formation.title: The Birth of Malaya
formation.text:
The Malay Peninsula stands united under a single sultanate for the first time since the great days of Malacca. The Straits stretch before us: the richest sea lane in all the world, where the riches of China, India, and the Spice Islands converge. Our court draws scholars and merchants from across the Islamic world, and the Hukum Kanun Melaka provides a legal framework admired from Gujarat to Guangzhou.

But what kind of state shall this new Malaya be? Shall we build upon our command of the Straits, turning every port into a warehouse of the world's trade, or shall we look inward to the strength of our faith and law, making the sultanate a model of Islamic governance that lesser rulers will emulate?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the gatekeepers of the Straits.

modifiers.name: Thalassocratic Emporium
modifiers.text: The Straits of Malacca are the crossroads of the known world, and we are their gatekeepers. Every vessel bearing silk from China, spices from the Moluccas, or cloth from India must pass through our waters. We shall build the greatest entrepot the world has ever seen.

options.text: We are the servants of God and the law.

modifiers.name: Sultanate of the Faithful
modifiers.text: From the Hukum Kanun Melaka to the madrasas that dot our cities, the Malay sultanate is a beacon of Islamic civilization in the eastern seas. Our legal codes govern trade and justice, our scholars illuminate the faith, and our Sultan rules as the shadow of God on earth.

advances.name: Orang Laut Alliance
advances.text: The Orang Laut, the sea people, are the eyes and arms of the sultanate upon the water. These seafaring nomads patrol the straits, repel pirates, and guide merchant vessels to our ports in exchange for royal patronage and titles.

advances.name: Hulubalang Tradition
advances.text: The Hulubalang are the elite warriors of the Malay court, sworn to the Sultan's service. Armed with the kris, the wavy-bladed dagger sacred to Malay martial culture, they serve as both palace guards and shock troops in battle.

advances.name: Entrepot System
advances.text: Malacca's genius was never production but redistribution. Goods from China, India, Arabia, and the Spice Islands converge in Malay warehouses before being reshipped across the known world.

advances.name: Adat Governance
advances.text: Before Islam and before the sultanate, the Malay world was governed by adat: customary law. These ancient traditions of consensus, reciprocity, and local authority form the foundation upon which the sultanate builds its administration.

advances.name: Istana Tradition
advances.text: The Istana, the royal palace, is the heart of Malay political life. Elaborate court ceremonies, strict protocol, and the ritual display of regalia reinforce the Sultan's divine mandate and the hierarchy of the realm.

advances.name: Bendahara-Laksamana System
advances.text: The Malay sultanate divides governance between the Bendahara, who administers domestic affairs and diplomacy, and the Laksamana, who commands the fleet and enforces maritime law. This dualistic system prevents any single official from accumulating too much power.

advances.name: Islamic Learning Centers
advances.text: Malacca is not merely a trading port: it is a center of Islamic scholarship where ulama from Arabia, India, and Java gather to teach and debate. The madrasas of the sultanate train scholars, jurists, and administrators who carry the faith across the archipelago.

advances.name: Undang-Undang Laut Melaka
advances.text: The Maritime Laws of Malacca regulate every aspect of seafaring life, from the authority of a ship's captain to the treatment of passengers and cargo. Compiled under royal authority, they represent the most sophisticated body of maritime law in Southeast Asia.

event.title: The Undang-Undang Laut Melaka
event.text:
The sea captains of the sultanate have gathered at the court of the Sultan to codify the maritime laws that govern our waters. The Undang-Undang Laut Melaka, the Maritime Laws of Malacca, will regulate everything from the duties of a ship's captain to the rights of passengers, from the division of salvage to the punishment of mutiny.

Compiled under the authority of the Laksamana, these laws draw on centuries of Malay seafaring wisdom and Islamic jurisprudence. They will define how trade is conducted across the Straits. The question is whether these laws should prioritize strict enforcement of tolls and anti-piracy patrols, or whether a more liberal approach, encouraging free passage and attracting merchants through fair dealing, would better serve the sultanate's interests.

options.text: The Laksamana shall enforce order upon these waters.

modifiers.name: Maritime Law Enforced
modifiers.text: The Undang-Undang Laut Melaka is enforced with an iron hand. Pirates are hunted, tolls are collected, and every vessel in our waters answers to the Laksamana.

options.text: Let merchants know the Straits are open to all who deal fairly.

modifiers.name: Maritime Law Liberalized
modifiers.text: The Undang-Undang Laut Melaka encourages free passage and fair dealing. Merchants from every nation know that the Straits are open to honest trade.

advances.name: Cosmopolitan Port
advances.text: Gujarati Muslims, Tamil Hindus, Chinese Buddhists, and Javanese merchants mingle freely in Malacca's markets. This tolerance of all faiths and cultures is not mere idealism: it is the secret to the port's commercial success.

advances.name: Penjajap Warships
advances.text: The penjajap is a long, narrow war galley designed for the shallow waters of the Straits. Fast under both sail and oar, these vessels excel at raiding, pursuit, and coastal warfare where deep-keeled European ships cannot follow.

advances.name: Lancaran Tradition
advances.text: The lancaran is a medium-sized Malay warship, faster than a jong but more heavily armed than a raiding perahu. Purpose-built for trade escort and anti-piracy operations, lancarans are the workhorses of the Malay fleet.

advances.name: Strait Defense Network
advances.text: Watchtowers and signal stations along the Straits allow the sultanate to monitor all maritime traffic and respond swiftly to threats. This network turns the narrow waters into a defensive asset rather than a vulnerability.

advances.name: Johor Successor State
advances.text: When Malacca fell, its heirs did not perish. The sultans of Johor carried forward the legitimacy and traditions of old Malacca, waging guerrilla warfare against foreign occupiers and maintaining the Malay claim to the Straits.

event.title: The Fall of Malacca and the Johor Successor
event.text:
Malacca, the jewel of the Straits, has been seized by a foreign power. Sultan Mahmud Shah, the last ruler of old Malacca, retreated south with his court and warriors to establish a new base at Johor. His sons would found the successor sultanates of Johor and Perak, each carrying forward the traditions and legitimacy of Malacca.

The Johor Sultanate, backed by the loyalty of the Orang Laut sea nomads and the memory of Malacca's greatness, wages a guerrilla campaign to deny the invaders control of the Straits. The jungle hinterland provides refuge, while Malay knowledge of coastal waters gives the sultans an advantage that no foreign fleet can easily overcome. The spirit of resistance burns bright.

options.text: Malacca may have fallen, but Malaya endures.

modifiers.name: Johor Resistance
modifiers.text: The fall of Malacca steeled our resolve. From Johor, the heirs of the sultanate wage a tireless campaign to reclaim what was lost, drawing strength from the jungle and the loyalty of the Malay people.

advances.name: Spice Redistribution
advances.text: Cloves from the Moluccas, pepper from Sumatra, cinnamon from Lanka: the spices of the East converge in Malay entrepots, where they are graded, repackaged, and shipped onward to the markets of India, Arabia, and beyond.

advances.name: Perak Tin Boom
advances.text: The alluvial tin deposits of Perak's river valleys are among the richest in the world. Chinese miners, Bugis middlemen, and Malay sultans all profit from the tin trade, which transforms the peninsula's economy.

event.title: The Tin of Perak
event.text:
Rich deposits of tin have been discovered in the river valleys of Perak. The metal, essential for pewter, bronze, and increasingly for industrial applications, flows from Perak's mines to the ports of the peninsula and from there to the world. The Malay tin trade transforms Perak from a quiet riverside sultanate into one of the wealthiest states in Southeast Asia.

Chinese miners flock to the diggings, Bugis traders handle the export, and the Sultan of Perak grows rich from the taxes levied on every ingot that leaves his territory. Tin joins spices and pepper as the pillars of the Malay economy.

options.text: Let the tin flow, and the wealth shall follow.

advances.name: Hukum Kanun Melaka
advances.text: The Hukum Kanun Melaka is a comprehensive legal code blending Islamic sharia with Malay customary law. It covers constitutional, criminal, commercial, and family law, providing the legal foundation for the sultanate's administration.

advances.name: Ghali Besar Tradition
advances.text: The Ghali Besar, the great galley, is the largest warship in the Malay fleet. Propelled by hundreds of oarsmen and bristling with swivel guns, these vessels defend the Straits against all comers.

advances.name: Rivalry Modernization
advances.text: Competition between the Malay sultanates (Johor against Aceh, Perak against Selangor) drives military innovation. Gunpowder weapons, professional soldiers, and European-influenced fortifications gradually replace older methods of war. Bronze swivel guns, the lela and the smaller rentaka, are cast in the ports and carried on campaign.

advances.name: Pelabuhan Tradition
advances.text: The pelabuhan, the great harbor, is more than a dock. It is a self-contained commercial district with warehouses, shipyards, customs houses, and quarters for merchants of every nation. Building a pelabuhan declares a port open to the world.

advances.name: Bugis Alliance
advances.text: The Bugis of Sulawesi are renowned as both fierce warriors and shrewd merchants. Their alliance with the Malay sultanates brings mercenary swords, trading expertise, and connections to the maritime networks of the eastern archipelago.

advances.name: Sultanate Court Patronage
advances.text: The Malay court nurtures a rich literary and artistic tradition. The Hikayat Hang Tuah, the Sejarah Melayu, and countless other works of poetry and history are composed under royal patronage, establishing the Malay language as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Global Pepper Trade
advances.text: Pepper from the interior of the Malay Peninsula and from Sumatran tributary states enters world markets through our ports. The demand from Europe, India, and China ensures that pepper remains one of the most valuable commodities in the Malay economy.

advances.name: Malay Diaspora Network
advances.text: Malay merchants and settlers are found from the coasts of India to the Philippines, from Siam to the Moluccas. This far-flung diaspora provides intelligence, commercial connections, and diplomatic leverage across maritime Asia.

advances.name: Modern Lancaran Fleet
advances.text: The lancaran tradition evolves with the times. Modern patrol vessels combine European rigging with Malay hull design, creating fast, versatile ships ideally suited for the shallow, island-studded waters of the Straits.

advances.name: Centralized Sultanate
advances.text: The Sultan tightens his grip on the reins of power, subordinating the Bendahara and Temenggung to direct royal authority. Provincial chiefs are replaced with appointed governors, and tax collection is systematized.

advances.name: Tin Smelting Industry
advances.text:
Chinese kongsi bring capital, chain pumps and thousands of miners to the tin fields of Perak, and the diggings go deeper and wider than the Malay miners ever worked them. The tin industry employs thousands and generates enormous revenue for the sultanate's treasury.

Available in: Kongsi Lombong

advances.name: Blockade Mastery
advances.text: Centuries of controlling the narrowest sea lane in Asia have given the Malay fleet an unmatched understanding of blockade warfare. No ship passes through the Straits without the Sultan's knowledge and consent.

advances.name: Silat Tradition
advances.text: Silat, the Malay martial art, is codified from its many regional variants into a formal discipline taught in royal courts and military schools. The graceful but deadly art emphasizes speed, leverage, and the lethal use of the kris.

advances.name: Nusantara Literary Renaissance
advances.text: The Malay language achieves its full flowering as the literary lingua franca of the archipelago. From the royal chronicles of the Sejarah Melayu to the romantic epics of the Hikayat tradition, Malay literature defines the cultural identity of the region.

advances.name: Modern Harbor Infrastructure
advances.text: Steam-powered cranes, deep-water berths, and warehouses built to European specifications transform Malay ports into modern commercial facilities capable of handling the massive volume of world trade that passes through the Straits.

advances.name: Malay National Awakening
advances.text: A new generation of Malay intellectuals, educated in both Islamic and Western traditions, articulates a vision of Malay national identity that transcends individual sultanates. The idea of a unified Malay nation takes root.

advances.name: Plantation Economy
advances.text: Chinese planters open gambier and pepper gardens in the forests of Johor and Riau under licences from the Malay chiefs. The gardens move on as the firewood around them runs out, and the pepper they ship carries the peninsula's trade beyond tin.

advances.name: Naval Modernization
advances.text: Steam-powered warships and modern artillery replace the galleys and lancarans of old. The Malay fleet adapts to the new era of naval warfare while retaining its mastery of the strait waters.

advances.name: Constitutional Sultanate
advances.text: The absolute power of the Sultan gives way to a constitutional framework that balances royal authority with the rights of the people. A modern bureaucracy administers the state, while the Sultan retains his role as symbol and religious guardian.

advances.name: Straits Settlements Integration
advances.text: The great ports of the peninsula (Malacca, Penang, Singapore) are bound together into an integrated economic zone. Unified customs, standardized weights, and coordinated shipping schedules turn the Straits into a single commercial entity.

destiny.name: Destiny of Malaya
destiny.text: The Malay Peninsula is united once more. Now the question is what this new Malaya shall become: a maritime empire spanning the seas, or a beacon of Islamic civilization illuminating the East. Stabilize the realm and set your course.

event.title: The Destiny of Malaya
event.text: The peninsula is united, the straits secured. But this is merely the beginning. A greater destiny awaits: one that will be shaped by the choices we make in the years ahead. The traditions of our ancestors light the way forward.

destiny.name: The Straits Gateway
destiny.text: Control both ends of the Straits of Malacca by seizing Palembang on Sumatra and Aceh at the western approach. With these great ports in our hands, no ship enters or leaves the Straits without Malay consent.

conditions.text: Own Palembang, or a subject owns it
Own Bandar Aceh, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Straits Gateway Secured
event.text: From Aceh in the west to Palembang in the south, the approaches to the Straits of Malacca are now under Malay control. Every merchant vessel bearing silk, spices, or porcelain must pass through waters where the Sultan's writ runs. The great entrepot system can now function at its full potential: no rival power can divert trade around us.

destiny.name: The Spice Monopoly
destiny.text: The fabulous wealth of the Spice Islands must flow through Malay hands alone. Seize Banda and Ternate, the twin hearts of the clove and nutmeg trade, and make our entrepots the sole gateway between East and West.

conditions.text: Own Banda, or a subject owns it
Own Ternate, or a subject owns it

event.title: Masters of the Spice Trade
event.text:
Banda and Ternate, the fabled Spice Islands, now answer to the Sultan of Malaya. The cloves, nutmeg, and mace that the world craves pass through our warehouses before reaching any foreign port. This monopoly grants us enormous power. But how shall we wield it?

We could build upon our diplomatic relationships, using trade to bind allies and subjects to us through prosperity. Or we could arm our merchant fleet, ensuring that any nation that dares challenge our monopoly will face the full force of Malay naval power.

options.text: Trade binds the world to us.

modifiers.name: Entrepot Dominance
modifiers.text: Our trade network binds nations to us through mutual prosperity. Every court in Asia knows that Malay friendship means access to the richest markets in the world.

options.text: Our merchants sail with cannons loaded.

modifiers.name: Armed Trade
modifiers.text: Our merchant vessels sail with guns loaded and crews battle-ready. The Malay trade monopoly is enforced not just by commercial superiority but by overwhelming naval force.

destiny.name: Nusantara Thalassocracy
destiny.text: From Makassar to Canton, every major port of the Eastern seas must answer to the Sultan of Malaya. Build the Emporium Agung, the Great Market, and prove that the age of the Malay thalassocracy has returned.

conditions.text: Own Gowa, or a subject owns it
Own Guǎngzhōu, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Nusantara Thalassocracy
event.text:
From the pepper gardens of Sumatra to the porcelain kilns of Guangzhou, from the tin mines of Perak to the clove groves of Ternate, the Malay thalassocracy spans the eastern seas. The Emporium Agung rises in our greatest port: a market of unimaginable scale where the wealth of three continents converges.

Shall we consolidate this empire through commerce and centralized administration, making our burghers the richest in the world? Or shall we assert ourselves as the unchallenged maritime hegemon, ensuring that our naval supremacy is beyond question?

options.text: Let the Emporium Agung stand as our monument.

modifiers.name: World Emporium
modifiers.text: The Emporium Agung stands as the greatest marketplace in the eastern world, a monument to Malay commercial genius where the burghers of a dozen nations trade under Malay law.

modifiers.name: Maritime Hegemon
modifiers.text: No fleet dares challenge Malay supremacy on the eastern seas. From the Straits of Malacca to the South China Sea, the Sultan's navy is the final arbiter of all maritime disputes.

destiny.name: The Hukum Kanun Proclaimed
destiny.text: Proclaim the Hukum Kanun Melaka as the universal legal code of the sultanate, blending Islamic sharia with Malay customary law. Grow Malacca from a fishing village into the town whose name the code carries, and let the world see that Malay justice is second to none.

conditions.text: We hold Malacca and it has grown into a town or become the seat of a market

event.title: The Hukum Kanun Proclaimed
event.text: In a great ceremony at the court of the Sultan, the Hukum Kanun Melaka is proclaimed as the universal legal code of the realm. Islamic sharia and Malay adat are woven together into a comprehensive system of law that governs commerce, family, criminal justice, and constitutional matters. Merchants from across the Indian Ocean recognize the fairness and sophistication of Malay courts.

options.text: Let justice reign in our lands.

destiny.name: Light of the Eastern Seas
destiny.text: Make the sultanate the foremost center of Islamic learning east of Baghdad. Found libraries in three of your towns to keep the Quran and legal scholarship. Ensure paper is traded in your capital's market: the ink of scholars is the lifeblood of civilization.

conditions.text: A Library stands in at least 3 of our towns

children.text: Paper is produced in the market
Paper is traded in the market

event.title: The Light of the Eastern Seas
event.text:
Scholars from Arabia, Persia, India, and Java flock to the madrasas of the sultanate. The copying of the Quran and legal commentaries in Jawi script in our libraries spreads Islamic learning to every corner of the archipelago. Our courts are renowned for their learning and our judges for their wisdom.

Shall we formalize the sharia court system, bringing Islamic jurisprudence to bear on every aspect of governance? Or shall we invest in expanding the madrasa network, making the sultanate the intellectual capital of the Islamic East?

options.text: The law shall be our foundation.

modifiers.name: Sharia Courts
modifiers.text: Formal sharia courts administer Islamic law across the sultanate, providing justice and stability while regulating commercial activity under divine guidance.

options.text: Knowledge is the truest form of worship.

modifiers.name: Madrasa Network
modifiers.text: An extensive network of madrasas educates the people of the sultanate in both religious scholarship and worldly sciences, pushing the frontiers of knowledge in the Islamic East.

destiny.name: Dar al-Islam of the Archipelago
destiny.text: The Malay sultanate stands as the undisputed heart of Islamic civilization in the eastern world. Keep madrasas in five of your towns, build Malacca up into a city worthy of the faith it carried across the archipelago, and complete the pilgrimage by bringing Mecca itself under your protection.

conditions.text: At least 5 of our locations have a Madrasa or a Malay Madrasa
Malacca is held and its development is at least 34
Own Mecca, or a subject owns it

event.title: Dar al-Islam of the Archipelago
event.text:
The sultanate has achieved what no other Muslim state east of Delhi has accomplished: the creation of a true Dar al-Islam spanning the seas from the Malay Peninsula to the holy cities of Arabia. The Darul Hukum rises as the ultimate expression of our commitment to Islamic governance.

Shall we use this position to centralize authority under the Sultan as Commander of the Faithful, subordinating the nobility to the divine law? Or shall we become a beacon of faith that lifts all our people through education, culture, and communal solidarity?

options.text: The Sultan is the shadow of God.

modifiers.name: Ummah United
modifiers.text: The Sultan rules as Commander of the Faithful, subordinating the old aristocratic order to the divine law. Spiritual authority flows from the crown, binding the ummah under a single righteous sovereign.

options.text: The faith belongs to all believers.

modifiers.name: Beacon of Faith
modifiers.text: The sultanate shines as a beacon of Islamic civilization, where communal solidarity and scholarly excellence lift all believers toward a more enlightened future.

units.name: Orang Laut Raider
units.text: The Orang Laut, the sea people, serve the Sultan as naval irregulars, using their intimate knowledge of coastal waters to patrol the straits, hunt pirates, and harry enemy shipping.

units.name: Hulubalang
units.text: The Hulubalang are the elite warriors of the Malay court. Armed with the sacred kris and trained in silat, they serve as both palace guards and shock infantry, their fanatical loyalty matched only by their skill in close combat.

units.name: Penjajap
units.text: A long, narrow war galley designed for the shallow waters of the Straits. The penjajap excels at fast raiding and coastal warfare, darting through channels where heavier vessels cannot follow.

units.name: Lancaran
units.text: A medium-sized Malay warship combining sail and oar power. The lancaran serves as the primary trade escort and anti-piracy vessel, fast enough to chase down raiders and well-armed enough to deter them.

units.name: Ghali Besar
units.text: The great galley of the Malay fleet, propelled by hundreds of oarsmen and armed with swivel guns. The Ghali Besar is the Sultan's instrument of naval authority over the Straits.

units.name: Modern Lancaran
units.text: An updated patrol vessel blending Malay shallow-draft design with modern rigging and armament. The modern lancaran maintains the traditional Malay advantage in strait and archipelagic waters.

units.name: Bugis Warrior
units.text: Fierce warrior-merchants from Sulawesi, the Bugis serve the Malay sultanates as both mercenary soldiers and trade intermediaries. Their charge and their skill at flanking are feared, though a band that sees the day going against it will break off.

units.name: Lela and Rentaka Battery
units.text: The lela and the smaller rentaka are bronze swivel guns cast in the Malay ports. Light enough to be carried by two men, they are mounted on stockades and on the gunwales of war boats and are quickly brought into action. Against stone walls they do little.

units.name: Pendekar
units.text: Master practitioners of silat, the Malay martial art. The Pendekar are elite warriors whose speed, technique, and lethal proficiency with the kris make them devastating shock infantry.

units.name: Modern Corvette
units.text: A steam-age patrol warship adapted to the shallow, island-studded waters of the Straits. Fast and agile, the modern corvette maintains the Malay tradition of maritime dominance into the industrial era.

buildings.name: Entrepot Warehouse
buildings.text: A massive warehouse complex where goods from across the known world are stored, graded, and reshipped. The entrepot warehouse is the physical infrastructure of the Malay middleman economy.

buildings.name: Istana
buildings.text: The Istana is the royal palace of a Malay sultanate, a center of political authority, ceremonial display, and cultural patronage. Its elaborate architecture and court rituals embody the majesty of the Malay ruling tradition.

buildings.name: Tin Smeltery
buildings.text: Smelting sheds at the river diggings, where the washed ore is smelted in charcoal furnaces and cast into slabs for the river boats. Smelting at the diggings lets the miners work more ground, and the tin field it stands on yields more.

where.text: The location's raw material is Tin

buildings.name: Kongsi Lombong
buildings.text: The open tin pit of a Chinese mining kongsi. A chain pump of wooden paddles, turned by a water wheel, drains the pit deep below the old washings, so the field holds more miners, and every season more come from China to work it.

where.text: The location's raw material is Tin

buildings.name: Malay Madrasa
buildings.text: An Islamic school where scholars study the Quran, jurisprudence, and the sciences. The madrasas of the Malay sultanate train the jurists, administrators, and religious leaders who govern the realm and spread the faith.

buildings.name: Strait Watchtower
buildings.text: A fortified observation post along the Straits of Malacca, enabling the sultanate to monitor maritime traffic, detect pirates, and coordinate naval patrols across its territorial waters.

buildings.name: Pelabuhan
buildings.text: A great harbor complex with deep-water berths, warehouses, shipyards, and customs facilities. The pelabuhan is the commercial gateway of the sultanate, open to merchants of every nation.

buildings.name: Plantation Estate
buildings.text: A gambier and pepper garden worked by Chinese planters under a Malay chief's licence. It diversifies Malaya's wealth beyond tin.

children.text: Pepper is produced in the market

buildings.name: Emporium Agung
buildings.text: The Great Market: a colossal trading complex where the goods of three continents converge. Silk from China, spices from the Moluccas, cloth from India, and silver from Japan change hands under a single roof governed by Malay commercial law.

buildings.name: Darul Hukum
buildings.text: The House of Law: a grand complex combining a supreme sharia court, a royal library, and a madrasa of the highest order. It is the institutional heart of Malay Islamic governance, where jurisprudence and scholarship serve the faith.

list.name: Bendahara Grand-Vizierate
list.text: The highest civilian office of the Melaka Sultanate, held in the kingdom's golden age by Tun Perak (c. 1456-1498), who as Bendahara directed the realm through five sultans, repulsed two Siamese invasions in 1456 and 1488, and ran the chancery, foreign affairs, and noble appointments from his residence at Bukit China. The office was hereditary in the Tun lineage; in practice the Bendahara was the de facto first minister while the sultan presided. The institution survived Melaka's fall: Johor's Bendaharas eventually founded the breakaway state of Pahang in 1770 and became sultans in their own right.

list.name: Laksamana Admiralty
list.text: The office of admiral-of-the-fleet, held in Melaka tradition by the famed Hang Tuah and his successors. The Laksamana commanded the royal kelulus, led the sultan's bodyguard of hulubalang, and policed the Straits against pirates and recalcitrant vassals from Pasai to Patani. After 1511 the institution moved with the sultan to Johor; its keris was held to the throat of any chief who failed to render tribute. The office persisted into the Bugis-Riau federation period as the Yam Tuan Muda's naval arm.

list.name: Hukum Kanun Melaka
list.text: The legal code compiled under Sultan Muzaffar Shah (r. 1446-1459) and refined under Mahmud Shah (r. 1488-1511), surviving in some thirty manuscript recensions across the Malay world. Its forty-four chapters fused Islamic shari'a with Malay adat, and the code was adopted as reference text by the later sultanates of Johor, Pahang, Kedah, and Patani. The companion Undang-Undang Laut Melaka, Mahmud Shah's maritime ordinance, governed shipboard authority, cargo disputes, and voyage profits, and was binding on every vessel sailing under Melaka registry from Mergui to Maluku.

list.name: Shahbandaria of the Four Quarters
list.text: The four port-officers of Melaka, each governing a chartered foreign trading community of the entrepot in Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental (c. 1515): the Shahbandar of the Gujaratis, the Shahbandar of the Tamils and Pegu, the Shahbandar of the Javanese and Maluku and Luzon, and the Shahbandar of the Chinese and Champa. Each collected import-duties at the published rate, assigned warehouse plots, settled disputes within his community by its own customary law, and represented his merchants to the Bendahara's chancery. The institution made Melaka governable for crown and merchant alike.

list.name: Orang Laut Tanah-Air Compact
list.text: The institutional understanding between the Malay throne and the Orang Laut sea-nomads of the Riau-Lingga and Tudjuh archipelagos, by which the sea-people held customary rights to specific territorial waters (tanah air, 'land and water') in exchange for naval service to the sultan. Attested in the Sejarah Melayu's account of Sang Nila Utama, the compact gave Melaka and Johor a body of pilots, irregular naval auxiliaries, and informants whose knowledge of every reef from Singapore to Lingga was unmatched. The Orang Laut suku of Bentan and Galang were the kingmakers of Johor: their shift to the Bugis Yam Tuan Muda in 1722 made the Bugis-Riau federation the dominant Malay polity.
